{"id": "1:3/q12", "question": "Why are both mercy names joined?", "turns_on": "Whether pairing reinforces one meaning or adds a distinct aspect and reassurance.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q12/p1", "position": "The pairing intensifies and completes the description of mercy.", "reasons": "Majāz's Arabic synonym pairs and poetry defend doubled expression; Jishumī says it intensifies mercy and traces every blessing to God. Quṭb and Study Quran say together they cover mercy's range."}, {"id": "1:3/q12/p2", "position": "The two forms unite continually renewed and permanently established mercy.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī says faʿlān suggests fresh fullness and faʿīl stable quality; either alone could suggest impermanence or mere stasis. Al-Tafsīr al-Qayyim compares anger and regret; examples include ghaḍbān, ʿaṭshān, ṭawīl, ḍaʿīf and 20:86."}, {"id": "1:3/q12/p3", "position": "The pairing identifies the formerly less familiar name with the God Arabs knew.", "reasons": "Jishumī says Allah was familiar but al-Raḥmān less so. Another report contrasts Torah's al-Raḥmān, Gospel's al-Raḥīm and Qur'an's Allah; Abū al-ʿAbbās contrasts shared Hebrew-Arabic al-Raḥmān with Arabic al-Raḥīm."}, {"id": "1:3/q12/p4", "position": "The second adds a broad recipient-directed meaning to the exclusive intrinsic first.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says 9:128 calls the Messenger raḥīm; repetition without new meaning would be rhetorically weak."}, {"id": "1:3/q12/p5", "position": "The second name makes small needs approachable after the exclusive majestic first.", "reasons": "Rāzī says humans might hesitate to ask the great Lord for a sandal strap or salt; a report has God invite Moses to request salt and fodder."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q13", "question": "Why does al-Raḥmān precede al-Raḥīm?", "turns_on": "Whether form strength, divine exclusivity, intrinsic priority, or immediacy determines order.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q13/p1", "position": "Its stronger, more exclusive, name-like form comes first.", "reasons": "Jishumī says stronger intensity and exclusivity make it more definite; Biqāʿī orders existence, general mercy, then worship-specific mercy. Ibn ʿĀshūr records most scholars' stronger faʿlān view, while noting the expected rhetorical increase from weaker to stronger. Al-Suyūṭī gives raʾūf then raḥīm as another instance of a less emphatic term following a stronger one."}, {"id": "1:3/q13/p2", "position": "An intrinsic attribute comes before its outward effects among recipients.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr makes essential character prior to the many objects of its mercy; 9:128 shows that the latter is also applied to the Messenger."}, {"id": "1:3/q13/p3", "position": "Immediate renewed mercy is mentioned first because people desire what comes soon.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī cites 75:20 and the contrast between faʿlān's renewed fullness and faʿīl's stability."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q14", "question": "How are the two names read and parsed in this verse?", "turns_on": "Case endings and whether the names continue the preceding construction or detach as praise.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q14/p1", "position": "Both are accusative as detached praise.", "reasons": "Abū al-ʿĀliya, Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ and ʿĪsā b. ʿUmar are named by Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū Ḥayyān; al-Ālūsī also names Zayd. Al-Naḥḥās allows an implied praising verb."}, {"id": "1:3/q14/p2", "position": "Both are nominative as detached praise or an implied subject.", "reasons": "Abū Razīn al-ʿUqaylī, al-Rabīʿ b. Khuthaym and Abū ʿImrān al-Jawnī are named by Ibn al-Jawzī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī."}, {"id": "1:3/q14/p3", "position": "Both are genitive, attached as adjectives or apposition.", "reasons": "The majority connect the names to preceding divine epithets; Abū Ḥayyān allows adjectival, appositional and explanatory appositional parses. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says joining the alif of al-ḥamdu may resolve adjacent consonants. Al-Zajjāj says their genitive follows the case of God's name while praising Him."}, {"id": "1:3/q14/p4", "position": "Mixed case endings are grammatically possible.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās allows one nominative and one accusative, or first genitive then second nominative or accusative."}, {"id": "1:3/q14/p5", "position": "An opened final mīm joined to an alif was heard, but not established as a transmitted reading.", "reasons": "Al-Kisāʾī cites an Arab's pronunciation; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says he knows no reading transmitter for it."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q15", "question": "What does mercy mean when attributed to God?", "turns_on": "Whether it names essential willing, acts of benefit, both, or humanlike feeling.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q15/p1", "position": "It means God's willing good and bringing benefit, without human emotional change.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī calls willing good an essential attribute. Elmalılı prefers both essential will and beneficent acts and distinguishes Turkish rahmet from merhamet. Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes affect from effective outcome, invokes 42:11 and 7:156, and says common use makes the divine sense clear, not ambiguous under 3:7; al-Ghazālī says mercy unable to produce its effect is incomplete."}, {"id": "1:3/q15/p2", "position": "It means the effect of mercy: rescue, gentleness and benefaction.", "reasons": "Exegetes reported by Elmalılı take the lexical transfer as an action attribute. Ibn ʿĀshūr says scripture directs ordinary language toward gentle action and aid rather than creaturely passion. Rāzī joins rescue from affliction and delivery of benefits."}, {"id": "1:3/q15/p3", "position": "The names are truly divine but their ultimate reality exceeds human knowledge.", "reasons": "Sulamī invokes 20:110 against claims to comprehend God's essence; Elmalılı says divine predication is literally true, though not identical to human feeling. Ibn ʿĀshūr says scriptural language expresses exalted meaning as ordinary language permits."}, {"id": "1:3/q15/p4", "position": "Divine mercy is the same tender emotion as human compassion.", "reasons": "Elmalılı and Ibn ʿĀshūr describe this human sense in order to rule it out for God, citing divine transcendence."}, {"id": "1:3/q15/p5", "position": "It means prior willing of good, an essential attribute.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī and some exegetes in Elmalılı's account distinguish divine will from human tenderness; Elmalılı says willing is choice, not emotional affect."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q16", "question": "What instances display the mercy named here?", "turns_on": "Which observed benefits, rescue, and apparent harms demonstrate its reach.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q16/p1", "position": "Mercy also guides ordinary need, communal welfare, and free striving.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr points to accessible earth, purification, good character, and zakāt benefiting society. Elmalılı describes life's provision, choice, a just balance and a hoped-for eternal good; 20:5 depicts encompassing sovereignty and 10:26 promises more to those who do good."}, {"id": "1:3/q16/p2", "position": "Creation, health, provision, insight, rescue, and even beneficial trials display mercy.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites medical discoveries, Galen's optic-nerve dream and vein cure, a raven feeding a bound man, a scorpion saving a youth, and gnats feeding a nestling. He argues schooling or amputation may hurt yet help, as al-Khiḍr's boat, boy and wall hide wisdom (18:79); worship disciplines the soul and Hell directs the wicked (17:7; 51:50). He says good generally exceeds evil and every atom testifies to mercy."}, {"id": "1:3/q16/p3", "position": "Mercy remains greater than even a loving mother or the Prophet's compassion.", "reasons": "Rāzī recounts the dying youth reconciled with his mother, asks how God could burn a long-believing servant, and contrasts the Prophet's finite compassion at the broken tooth, debt funeral and slander with God's limitless mercy."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q17", "question": "How can divine mercy coexist with evil, punishment, and human choice?", "turns_on": "Whether the names fit created disbelief and Hell, and how God and humans share agency.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q17/p1", "position": "Trials and punishment may serve a wise mercy judged by their ultimate effect.", "reasons": "Rāzī distinguishes appearance from reality: slight harm can enable greater good, religious duties purify, and al-Khiḍr's acts seemed objectionable to Moses. Elmalılı says harm follows nonexistence, divided wills and false partnership; mercy orders a society otherwise ruined and keeps recompense just."}, {"id": "1:3/q17/p2", "position": "God creates human capacities while people choose their striving under His continuing rule.", "reasons": "Elmalılı rejects both absolute determinism and autonomous creation. His examples are sudden paralysis, former Pharaohs' helplessness, and the limited, borrowed character of human authority; necessity witnesses divine power and choice divine will."}, {"id": "1:3/q17/p3", "position": "The Qadariyya question how mercy fits eternal Hell, created unbelief, and blocked faith.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports their objections without resolving them in that note."}, {"id": "1:3/q17/p4", "position": "The Jabriyya say God must create faith, the greatest mercy.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports their argument that if humans created faith, they would deserve these divine mercy names."}, {"id": "1:3/q17/p5", "position": "Humans have absolute future control after God delegates creation's course.", "reasons": "Elmalılı raises this idea only to reject it as confusing temporary agency with independent ownership and as the root of injustice."}]}

{"id": "1:3/q19", "question": "Why do the mercy names follow 'Lord of the worlds'?", "turns_on": "How lordship, mercy, fear, praise, and worship cohere in the sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q19/p1", "position": "Mercy softens the awe of lordship and gives hope that supports obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī cites 15:49-50 and 40:3 and a Muslim report that full knowledge of punishment or mercy would overwhelm hope or despair. Abū Ḥayyān says God's control makes mercy apt, and rejects alternatives 'constant one' or 'companion' for rabb; Sāmarrāʾī says a real nurturer should be merciful, citing 9:128."}, {"id": "1:3/q19/p2", "position": "Mercy explains and completes lordly nurture, giving reason to continue praise.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says lordship lacks full wellbeing without mercy and the names detail praise twice over. Ibn ʿĀshūr says weak creatures need gentle completion; benefits and duties can be arduous, so the name assures easing and public good. Al-Ālūsī says immense mercy follows universal nurture. Biqāʿī relates al-Raḥmān to lordship in both creations and al-Raḥīm especially to the second creation's preservation, recompense, and special mercy."}, {"id": "1:3/q19/p3", "position": "The order of lordship, mercy, and judgment is the best rational or rhetorical sequence.", "reasons": "Rāzī calls it unsurpassable. Al-Taftāzānī maps first creation to rabb, preservation to mercy, second creation to judgment, and afterlife preservation to subsequent worship. Bursevī maps creation, nurture, concealment, forgiveness and judgment. Study Quran puts mercy between sovereignty over space and mastery of time; Sāmarrāʾī spans eternity through afterlife."}, {"id": "1:3/q19/p4", "position": "The words describe God's praiseworthy perfections and prepare the servant to worship.", "reasons": "Burhān traces successive exclusive praise, universal lordship, mercy and judgment into seeking help. Al-Ālūsī lists inherent perfection, past benefit, future kindness and feared power; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the names legislative mercy; Sāmarrāʾī ties the guidance plea to lordship, mercy and reliance."}, {"id": "1:3/q19/p5", "position": "The mercy names are God's self-praise after the creation description.", "reasons": "Qatāda calls this verse God praising Himself; Durr al-Manthūr connects it with Lord of the worlds and the coming judgment."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q20", "question": "Why do the mercy names recur after the basmala?", "turns_on": "Whether the basmala belongs to the sūra, or each occurrence has a distinct rhetorical task.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q20/p1", "position": "The basmala and this verse serve distinct functions, so recurrence is purposeful.", "reasons": "ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā and al-Rummānī say the first ties servitude to blessings and the second praise to blessings. Al-Ālūsī says the basmala explains beginning in God's name while this verse explains His right to praise. Al-Bayḍāwī calls it causal explanation; Abū Ḥayyān says, if the basmala is in the sūra, attributes gain reinforcement."}, {"id": "1:3/q20/p2", "position": "The recurrence deliberately emphasizes the importance and breadth of mercy.", "reasons": "Jishumī lists emphasis as one explanation; al-Rāzī says Qur'anic repetition is common and mercy deserves special stress before judgment (40:3). Study Quran says the names intensify mercy, while Biqāʿī invokes al-Ghazālī's principle that no Qur'anic repetition is redundant."}, {"id": "1:3/q20/p3", "position": "The apparent repetition indicates the basmala is outside the Fātiḥa.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says adjacent complete verses would repeat without real separation and cites Jarīr and 18:1-2 for fronted semantic order; Makkī and al-Nasafī say al-ḥamdu does not truly separate them. Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects appeals to mere emphasis and al-Bayḍāwī's praise explanation."}, {"id": "1:3/q20/p4", "position": "The two names were already explained under the basmala.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr and Kur'an Yolu refer readers to earlier commentary; Abū Ḥayyān calls them praise epithets following the unique name."}, {"id": "1:3/q20/p5", "position": "There is no repeated basmala in recitations that omit it; the names introduce a title.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum notes rites without a basmala, so this verse emphatically introduces the mercy title."}, {"id": "1:3/q20/p6", "position": "The names' first occurrence seeks aid; their second assigns praise.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this distinction alongside the outside-sūra and emphasis explanations."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q21", "question": "How does the verse's order relate to nearby praise and sovereignty?", "turns_on": "Whether to retain the recited order or move mercy beside praise and kingship beside lordship.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q21/p1", "position": "The recited order builds from lordship through mercy to judgment and worship.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān rejects Makkī's reordered analysis, arguing that lordship and mercy precede dominion and worship. Rāzī calls the order rationally optimal; Biqāʿī says mercy completes lordship; al-Ālūsī says descriptions explain prior praise and prepare prayer."}, {"id": "1:3/q21/p2", "position": "Mercy belongs semantically beside praise and kingship beside lordship.", "reasons": "An exegetical group cited by al-Ṭabarī and Makkī in Abū Ḥayyān place mālik next to rabb and mercy next to al-ḥamdu; al-Ṭabarī says Arabic permits such fronting and cites Jarīr and 18:1-2."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q22", "question": "What response does God give when this verse is recited in prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q22/p1", "position": "God calls the recitation an act of extolling or magnifying Him.", "reasons": "Abū Hurayra's prophetic and non-prophetic versions, Jābir's divine saying, and reports through Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, al-Rāzī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Durr, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, Abū Dāwūd and Study Quran vary in whether the basmala glorifies, whether Mālik glorifies or entrusts, and how the rest is divided. Baghawī grades his version sound; al-Biqāʿī cites Muslim and the four Sunan. The central answer is praise for al-ḥamdu, extolling for the mercy names, and a granted petition."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q23", "question": "What do these names imply about God's relation to creatures?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q23/p1", "position": "God's bond with creatures is comprehensive mercy and care, eliciting praise, trust and affection.", "reasons": "Quṭb contrasts Greek and Babel portrayals of capricious gods and calls mercy a foundational worldview principle. Rāzī speaks of complete generosity before and after death; Sāmarrāʾī reads the names as total mercy in both worlds; al-Bayḍāwī says invocation seeks assistance and mercy for righteous action."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q24", "question": "What devotional uses of these words are reported?", "turns_on": "Hope in frequent recitation versus supplication for rain.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q24/p1", "position": "Their frequent recitation gives hope of divine rescue.", "reasons": "Rāzī compares Mary's rescue from slander through one mercy (19:21) with worshippers reciting the names 34 times daily."}, {"id": "1:3/q24/p2", "position": "They were used in a drought prayer for sustaining rain.", "reasons": "A report from ʿĀʾisha names God Lord of the worlds, Merciful and Master of Judgment; Abū Dāwūd calls it rare with a good chain and says it supports the Medinan no-alif reading."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q25", "question": "What commentary do the divine names require?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q25/p1", "position": "They call for explanation of meaning, majesty, divine attributes, and placement.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Jamra says a commentary must explain the two names, all divine names and attributes, and why these occur here."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q26", "question": "Is the basmala counted as a Fātiḥa verse?", "turns_on": "How recitation, verse division, and repetition bear on the first verse.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q26/p1", "position": "Yes, it is counted as verse one.", "reasons": "Umm Salama and a separate attribution to ʿĀʾisha count the basmala first, the mercy names third, and Mālik fourth. Ibn ʿĀshūr gives Medina's count, which instead separates 'those You favored,' and notes the opening revelation report's omission of the formula (96:1)."}]}

{"id": "1:3/q29", "question": "Why is the Fātiḥa called the Opening or Mother of the Book?", "turns_on": "Whether the titles refer to placement, prayer, or a synopsis of the Qur'an.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q29/p1", "position": "Mother names its gathering of the Qur'an's major purposes.", "reasons": "Rāzī lists theology, resurrection, prophecy, decree; praise, service and requests; lordship and servitude; theology, duties and purification. Ibn ʿĀshūr debates whether the title is descriptive annexation or true annexation to the rest of the Book; Study Quran includes opening the heart to faith."}, {"id": "1:3/q29/p3", "position": "Other titles name its praise, prayer, cure, sufficiency, thanks and supplication.", "reasons": "Rāzī explains Sūrat al-Ḥamd by its first praise word. {"id": "1:3/q30", "question": "What is meant by the worlds whose Lord is named before this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether worlds include every existent, only rational beings, eras, or enumerated realms.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q30/p1", "position": "All creatures and existents apart from God.", "reasons": "Qatāda says ʿālamūn has no singular of the same form; al-Qurṭubī prefers the broadest view, citing Pharaoh's question and the heavens and earth in 26:23-24. Al-Zajjāj and al-Khalīl derive the word from a sign pointing to the Creator."}, {"id": "1:3/q30/p2", "position": "Rational creatures, especially humans and jinn.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās cites 25:1 for humans and jinn; al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda include angels and devils because this plural designates rational beings; other reports include provisioned or spiritual beings."}, {"id": "1:3/q30/p3", "position": "People of each age.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥusayn b. al-Faḍl cites 26:165 as evidence for an era's people."}, {"id": "1:3/q30/p4", "position": "There are 18,000 worlds.", "reasons": "Wahb b. {"id": "1:3/q31", "question": "What is the Fātiḥa's larger structure and purpose?", "turns_on": "How its praise, mercy, judgment, worship and guidance organize the sūra and its relation to the Qur'an.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q31/p1", "position": "It proceeds from divine praise and attributes to worship, then the servant's need for guidance.", "reasons": "Rāzī maps refuge, basmala, praise, lordship, mercy, judgment, worship and avoidance of error; Quṭb and Study Quran group God's nature, relation, and human states. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a literary preface preparing hearers to cast off obstinacy; Biqāʿī and al-Ḥarālī call it the Qur'an's condensed universals and watchfulness."}, {"id": "1:3/q31/p2", "position": "Its diverse verses make purposeful, inimitable guidance rather than needless length.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī answers critics who claim judgment and worship already contain its meaning: the Qur'an gathers earlier scriptures' admonition and praise, adds commands, warnings, stories, arguments and parables, and its unmatched short-sūra composition certifies prophethood. The Fātiḥa moves listeners to gratitude, reliance on God and fear of sin."}, {"id": "1:3/q31/p3", "position": "Its arrangement is inimitable and obligatory in the recited order.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī cites al-Iṣfahānī on inimitable order and says rearranging or inserting foreign matter in prayer invalidates the recitation."}, {"id": "1:3/q31/p4", "position": "Al-Baqara answers its final guidance request.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says the next sūra presents the Book as guidance, models pious and astray groups, and stresses resurrection and inward faith; its cow story, hardened hearts and titles Radiant and Hump fit those themes."}]}
{"id": "1:3/q32", "question": "How does the sūra encompass scripture and its themes?", "turns_on": "How its brief expressions imply the Qur'an's whole range and earlier revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "1:3/q32/p1", "position": "It includes the Qur'an's central theology, duties, wisdom, and outcomes.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī divides contents into praise, worshipful command, promise and warning; al-Bayḍāwī gives theoretical wisdom, practical rulings and destinies. RAZI-FULL (القدرية): The Qadariyya argue that seeking assistance only makes sense if the servant can already perform the basic act; otherwise another's help is useless. ABUHAYYAN (الحسن، وأبو مجلز، وأبو المتوكل): Al-Ḥasan, Abū Majliz, and Abū al-Mutawakkil read iyyāka yaʿbudu with yāʾ and a passive verb. ABUHAYYAN (زيد بن علي، ويحيى بن وثاب، وعبيد بن عمير الليثي): Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb, and ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī read naʿbud with kasra on its initial nūn. ABUHAYYAN (author): The change to wāw reflects aversion to hamza; this reverses the alternative tendency to replace a kasra-bearing wāw with hamza. ABUHAYYAN (الجمهور): The majority read iyyā with a kasra on hamza and a doubled yāʾ. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (الحسن، وأبو مجلز، وأبو المتوكل): Al-Ḥasan, Abū Majlaz, and Abū al-Mutawakkil read iyyāka yaʿbud in the passive voice. ABUHAYYAN-FULL (author): Some read the direct address in iyyāka as an answer to deniers of time, God, or a creator, because it addresses a present existent. SAMIN-DURR (author): A dialect reads the imperfect prefix with kasra under stated conditions: not before yāʾ, and with a past stem having medial kasra, initial hamzat al-waṣl, or a reflexive tāʾ; ordinary forms such as yaḍribu lack these conditions. SAMIN-DURR (author): The common form has kasra and doubled y; other forms open the hamza or replace it with hā', with doubled or plain y, as a poem shows. SAMIN-DURR (author): Some reject the light pronunciation because it could sound like we worship your sun; the text notes irregular readings among the variants without detailing them. DURR (علي): Abu Razin reports Ali's pronunciation of this phrase with hamza, lengthening, and gemination. DURR-FULL (علي): Ali recited “You alone we worship … guide us” with both verbs raised; another report says he used hamza, lengthening, and shadda in “iyyaka.” ITQAN (ابن الحاجب): Ibn al-Hajib rejects the usual restrictive reading of a fronted complement as an illusion, citing the command to worship God sincerely and then the fronted “rather, worship God.” BURSEVI (النجمي): The Najmiyya reading says the shift from speaking of God to addressing Him directly occurs when the seeker crosses the veil of owning the self. ALUSI (الجمهور): The majority read iyyāka with a kasra on the hamza and a doubled yāʾ. ALUSI (القدرية): The Qadariyya argue that asking for aid makes sense only if the servant already has some capacity to act; without it, aid would be pointless. ALUSI (عبيد بن عمير الليثي وزيد بن حبيش ويحيى بن وثاب والنخعي): ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr al-Laythī, Zayd ibn Ḥubaysh, Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb, and al-Nakhaʿī read the initial nūn of naʿbudu with a kasra, a dialect of Qays, Tamīm, Asad, Rabīʿa, and Hudhayl. ALUSI-FULL (القدرية): The Qadariyya argue that asking help makes sense only if a person already has the capacity to perform the act. ALUSI-FULL (author): Al-Alusi's own subtle reading links the turn after Judgment Day to the believer's future delight in God's presence, direct conversation, and unveiling, a mercy paired with the preceding warning. ALUSI-FULL (رسول الله): A sound hadith to Ibn ʿAbbās commands him: when seeking help, seek God's help; al-Alusi sees it as evidence for the unrestricted reading. ELMALILI (author): The exclusive restriction here concerns asking for help; the omitted complement permits three readings: aid itself, aid in every matter, or aid in a specific matter.
